note: An entry is added when a version actually ships. Each one carries what it was accepted on, so a claim here can be checked rather than taken.

releases.title: The settlement gateway serves on p4
releases.body: gate.kvasir-ai.net answers again, this time against the p4 engine. A paid request crosses the gateway, the bridge and the MI250 ring and is billed on the tokens it actually used, not on an estimate. /v1/models answers 401 without a key — that is the gateway working, not an outage.
evidence: A prompt sent from a Galaxy S25 Ultra returned an answer billed at 28 tokens, and the credit balance moved by that amount.
The settlement ledger credited the bridge and both ring stages for the same request, each to its owner wallet.

releases.title: 28-31 tokens a second on a 428B model, and it stays there
releases.body: Two stages of Step-3.7-Flash on one MI250 machine decode at 28-31 tokens a second single stream, first token in 270-285 ms. The figure that matters is the second half: it no longer decays. The agent's journal used to be re-listed from disk before every record it wrote, so a ring got slower the longer it ran — 22.90 falling to 12.58 over four consecutive runs.
evidence: Six consecutive 100-token runs after the fix: 30.04, 31.21, 28.21, 29.04, 27.84, 28.73 tokens a second.
Padding the journal with 20,000 zero-byte entries, which charge nothing against its byte budget, used to take decode from 9.52 to 2.23 tokens a second. After the fix the same padding costs nothing.
Still holding 28 tokens a second at 19,761 journal entries, where before the fix it would have been under one.

releases.title: A device can prove a wallet and join the market
releases.body: The bridge serves the participation surface the mobile clients have been calling since the old control plane was retired: a wallet signature becomes a node token, the token buys an answer to what is under-covered, and a claimed window wires a relay so a device behind carrier NAT can be reached. What is not served yet is the shard download that would hand a device its weights, and the p4 engine has no path for dispatching expert work to a remote device at all.
evidence: Walked end to end against production with a freshly generated wallet: challenge, a 30-day node token, an assignment of layer 0 experts [0,32) with n_embd 4096, and a coverage claim that wired its relay session to a coordinator port.
The ring's one-byte role preamble crosses the relay untouched, with a test that fails if it does not.

releases.title: A 428B MoE placed across two machines
releases.body: Step-3.7-Flash — 428B parameters, 45 layers, 288 experts per layer with top-8 routing, Q4_K_XL at about 114 GiB — is placed as 16 stages across two AMD MI250 machines and serves from there. Placement comes from an operator's plan; the engine does not load a model because an HTTP call asked it to.
evidence: Both agents report their stages loaded at the same generation, verified by INSPECT rather than by a status page.
Eight GPUs per machine, 64 GiB each.

releases.title: The engine that replaced linkcpp
releases.body: p4 supersedes linkcpp as the engine behind the network. It keeps the data plane close to upstream and moves placement, session identity and the numbers a biller needs out of the engine and into an operator's hands.
evidence: One host, a 35B model: 512 of 512 requests completed, best 313.8 tok/s.
1,536 tests passing, 0 failing, in the public engine.
Source-available under BSL 1.1 on the p4 branch.

releases.title: Three machines, one model, one of them a phone
releases.body: Qwen3.5-122B served end to end across a GB10 and two Mac M4 Pros, with a Galaxy S25 holding part of the same model. Mixed backends produced matching tokens.
evidence: Cosine similarity of at least 0.9999 across ROCm, CUDA and a phone CPU.
Only hidden states crossed the network — no weights, no KV cache.
